title: The settlement of East Polynesia: the long pause, then the burst, c. 1000–1300
summary: After nearly two thousand years in West Polynesia, voyagers in double-hulled canoes went east to the Cook and Society Islands about 1000–1100, and from there, in some two centuries, to every corner of the Polynesian Triangle: Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa, and on to the Chathams and the subantarctic Auckland Islands. Oral traditions name founding navigators, such as Kupe for Aotearoa and Hotu Matuʻa for Rapa Nui; they are not datable people.

events.label: Rarotonga, the southern Cook Islands
events.text: The end of the long pause. For nearly two thousand years after Samoa nobody went further east; then, about 1000, someone did. Whether a run of El Niño westerlies or a better canoe opened the way is still argued.

events.label: Taputapuātea, Raʻiatea
events.text: The Society Islands, the first East Polynesian settlement with a good date, and in tradition the centre the voyaging canoes went out from.

events.label: Nuku Hiva, the Marquesas
events.text: Settled in the burst, and in some accounts the way north to Hawaiʻi.

events.label: Hawaiʻi
events.text: Some 4,000 km north of Tahiti, across the equator. Tradition names Hawaiʻiloa as its finder and Paʻao as a later priest from Tahiti. Whether it was settled before 1200 is disputed. The voyage of the Hōkūleʻa in 1976, by the stars and swells alone, settled the old argument that such voyages were made on purpose, not by drifting.

events.label: Mangareva
events.text: On the way east to Pitcairn and Rapa Nui, and the centre of a trade in stone tools across the islands of the far southeast.

events.label: Rapa Nui
events.text: The far eastern corner of the Triangle, settled about 1200. Tradition names Hotu Matuʻa as the founding chief.

events.label: Contact with South America
events.text: The sweet potato (kumara) is from South America, and it was grown across Polynesia before any European came. Native American DNA in Polynesians, dated to about 1200, shows the two peoples met. Whether South Americans reached Polynesia or Polynesians reached South America is not known.

events.label: Wairau Bar, Aotearoa
events.text: One of the earliest burial grounds in Aotearoa. Those buried first were born elsewhere, most likely in the islands to the north: the founders themselves. Tradition names Kupe as the first to find the land.

events.label: Rēkohu, the Chatham Islands
events.text: Settled from Aotearoa by the people who became the Moriori; the date is uncertain.

events.label: Enderby Island, the Auckland Islands
events.text: The southernmost camp Polynesians are known to have made, at 50° S, described by Atholl Anderson in 2005, and not lived in for long.
